facts: The petitioner is aggrieved by the order whereby his prayer for quashing the order taking cognizance u/s. 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and issuing process has been declined.
When the petitioner was posted as the Superintendent of District Jail, Bihar Sharif, the Food Inspector visited the jail premises and collected samples of various materials including Haldi and Rice.
Those articles were stored for consumption of the prisoners.

The samples so collected were sent for examination and analysis and, according to the report of the Public Analyst, Haldi and Rice were not found in conformity with the prescribed standard and, therefore, held to be adulterated.
Accordingly, two separate prosecution reports were submitted alleging commission of an offence u/s. 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act').
The learned Chief Judicial Magistrate took cognizance of the offence u/s. 16(1)(a) of the Act and by order dated 18th of March, 2006 directed for issuance of process in both the cases.
The petitioner assailed both the orders in separate revision applications filed before the Sessions Judge; but both were dismissed.

Thereafter, the petitioner preferred two separate applications, being Criminal Miscellaneous No. 15527 of 2010 and Criminal Miscellaneous No. 15471 of 2010 u/s. 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the High Court.
The High Court, by the orders impugned in the present special leave petitions, has dismissed both the criminal miscellaneous applications.
issues: Whether the expression 'store' as used in S. 7 and S. 16 of the Act would mean storage simplicitor or storage for sale.
petitioner_arguments: He submits that according to the prosecution report, these food items were not stored for sale and, therefore, the allegations made do not come within the mischief of S. 16(1)(a) of the Act.

He submits that the appellant at the relevant time was the Superintendent of Jail and food items which have been found to be adulterated were not stored for sale but were meant for consumption of the inmates.
court_reasoning: From a plain reading of the aforesaid provision, it is evident that S. 7 prohibits a person to 'manufacture for sale' or 'store' or 'sell' or 'distribute', inter alia, any adulterated food.

A conjoint reading of the aforesaid provisions makes it clear that the Food Inspector has the power to take sample of any article of food from any person selling such article under sub-s. (1) whereas sub-s. (2) confers on him the power to enter and inspect any place where any article of food is manufactured, stored or exposed for sale and take samples of such articles of food for analysis.
In our opinion, the term 'store' shall take colour from the context and the collocation in which it occurs in S. 7 and 16 of the Act.
holding: We allow these appeals, set aside the impugned orders and quash the appellant's prosecution in both the cases.
